A bit of a slog. Coming off of Batman the animated series. Nolan's imagining of a grounded batman universe is hellishly drab and heterosexual. As potentially interesting as the Joker performance is, the absense of camp does the character a big disservice, and the rivalry (or lack there of) lacks a lot of the charisma present in other renditions, in favor of something that feels much more generic (though maybe thats just me feeling inundated with the performance's shadow over the past decade of nerd and incel culture). The movie feels bloated, long, and with lots of fat to cut.

It felt as though we were rushing through every plot point to get to the next action scene. The script felt like a first draft, as do all Nolan films I have seen. Granted, many scenes with Joker were tense, yet this was mainly due to the score. What the fuck is Batman's new Batcave, like, what is this built for? Are you telling me this man spends all his time outside at night in the dark then returns back to a room with a ceiling brighter than the sun? fuck off. All characters felt only like caricatures, I knew fuck all about them and could barely care. I like Harvey Dent the most and his coin, but only because the comics did him so well, none of that felt like Nolan's work. Also the fuck was his bandaging, most dogshit I have ever seen. That will get infected little bro. Not to mention the scarecrow looked fucking ridiculous in the beginning. Nolan's urge to make everything seriously and manly made him look like a child in a suit. You gave him the mask, give him the rest of the fucking costume you coward. Wait.... no then we couldn't take it seriously nvm Nolan once again refuses to write women. Why would Jim's wife stay with him after he pulled that shit? He isn't even home in the first place. Furthermore, Gotham has no character in this movie. In the comics I have read along with The Batman Gotham has character. All we get here are establishing helicopter shots of NYC followed by more helicopter shots of NYC fucking MOVE ON ITS SO BORING I CANT. We genuinely stopped watching like 10 minutes before the end, because none of us cared. Most overrated movie I have ever seen. I'm the joker baby

The Joker is one of my all time least favourite comic book characters and most of that is because of the impact this movie had on the cultural consciousness. The “agent of chaos” characterisation is just. so. tedious. How does the Joker achieve anything in this film? He magically has everything he needs in exactly the right place like some Joker ex machina. And he’s so annoying. Sure, this is a good performance by Heath Ledger, but he’s performing an exhausting and irritating nuisance so I can’t say I enjoyed watching him. As annoying as it is, at least the Joker actually HAS a character. Everyone else in this is just a wooden puppet being pulled around on strings into big, boring set pieces. Oh, and the only female character of note gets fridged to develop the men. Classic Nolan! Also, I don’t really buy into the whole “superheroes are right-wing propaganda” thing some people have about the genre, but this is definitely right-wing propaganda.

We commonly criticize Hollywood action fare for being dumb but the far far more infuriating thing to me about this (and about a lot of Nolan movies tbh) is how hard it tries to have the superficial appearance of being a smart movie that is about something. Early on in the film a copycat Batman asks the real one “what makes you different from me?” and the Joker is introduced as an ideological foil to Batman, as another character willing to use extrajudicial means to advance a personal agenda. The copycat Batman asks a good question! And the rest of the movie circles around it, seemingly exploring themes of vigilantism, legitimacy, force, or community- I say seemingly because it sets up that these might be interesting avenues to use the character of Batman to explore…. and then doesn’t. By the end, the only real justification of Batman offered by THE DARK KNIGHT is that he’s a rich guy with military hardware and that nobody can stop him. The movie spends so much effort asking the question and being self reflexive that I can’t help but be bothered by this “lesson.” The movie itself is expanding on the core idea of BEGINS- “what if Batman existed in the real world?” by asking a new question: “Isn’t the idea of Batman kind of stupid?”

After watching the first two films of this trilogy, there's a thing that recurred, and tbh in any Nolan film I ever watched -aside from fascist propaganda- which is that there's not a single shot of any subtextual meaning anywhere in here; something that requires the audience to "read between the lines" rather than relying on characters directly stating their feelings, avoiding on the nose dialogue creates psychological depth and i long to see the day i see this thing in a Nolan movie. another thing that bothered me is that this movie relays on dialogue designed to establish themes, believing it can exploit their value to make the rest of the movie seem to dive into those ideas but it doesn't, the movie features famous lines about heavy topics but uses these dramatic speeches as a shortcut. It wants the audience to think the whole story is a deep exploration of those ideas, even when the plot itself is just a standard action movie. It's like a Michael Mann movie without any sauce. I think the main issue is while Mann's movies show such reverence and interest in its characters, Nolan could care less about fleshing his characters out beyond the first dimension so he can fit in more explosions and car chases. But don't worry, characters say Reddit philosophy quotes every other sentence so this movie is actually really deep and thought-provoking. Back to the characters, I find this to be the movie's biggest shortcoming. While Heath Ledger gives a fantastic performance as the Joker, the script he's working with offers him little help. Nolan's depiction of the Joker is so bland - he's an agent of chaos who does crime because he finds it fun. That's it. We never learn a thing about the Joker outside of his relationship to Batman. And that type of character can work. Anton Chigurh is a fantastic villain who fits a similar archetype to the Joker. But Chigurh works because we see the impact he has on the other characters in No Country for Old Men - how his nihilistic lack of motivation chills Ed to his core and makes him question everything he's been led to believe. But Batman/Bruce Wayne has no real character arc in this movie. In the first act his a bland superhero who beats up the bad guys, and in the third act he's still a bland superhero who beats up the bad guys. He learns nothing. He never grows. He never reflects on what the Joker represents, just chases him over and over until he finally catches him with the help of his cool gadgets. So what's the moral here? Batman just needed more gadgets to beat the Joker? The other characters in this film are of little interest either. Harvey Dent is a white knight ruthless prosecutor who chases down the bad guys and beats them up. Then he gets blown up and his world gets turned upside down because he chases down the people who wronged him and shoots them. I feel like this could be an interesting commentary on the criminal justice system being the other side of the coin of criminality itself, but the film is so afraid of depicting law enforcement with a shred of scrutiny that it plays it all completely straight. Harvey Dent is not a depiction of the corruption inherent in law enforcement, he's an awesome, flawless hero to all who is tragically brought down by the Joker. Because corruption isn't inherent in the system, rather it's propagated by a few bad apples like the Joker and his goons. How can I say this all so definitively? Because the movie tells us it definitively. It leaves nothing up to interpretation and tells us exactly what we should take away from each scene. "You either die a hero or live long enough to become the villain," "Some men just want to watch the world burn," etc. When characters aren't directly talking about what's happening in the scene or beating each other up, they're telling the audience what they should take away from the scene. Nolan's writing is so unsubtle I'm surprised he doesn't have Joker hold up a sign that says "I'm the bad guy." I genuinely have no idea why this film is so beloved. Maybe because it was such a shock in 2008 to see a superhero movie that's actually dark. But if you ignore the superhero dressing and analyze this film for what it is - a crime film - it just doesn't do anything to stand out among the plethora of far better crime films that have come before and since.

Eric Roberts’ filmography is fascinating. From this awful film to the cinematic masterpiece that is A Talking Cat!?! by gay soft-core porn legend David DeCoteau. Christopher Nolan wishes he was that talented The Dark Knight is one of those films which has such a huge following that any negative opinions of it feel automatically contrarian. I hate that, because I should feel safe saying how dull, unimaginative, and outright pathetic this movie feels. I truly do not understand why anybody likes this as a Batman film, let alone considering it as one of the greatest movies ever made. I will never say that something is “objectively” bad but I will confidentially say that Christopher Nolan objectively doesn’t understand Batman There’s no nuance, the fight choreography and editing throughout is total ass, no one is giving a good performance and dear god the pacing flows like a traffic jam. “Oh but Heath Ledger’s performance as the Joker is incredible” it really isn’t. Even if it was a good performance the characterisation is so butchered it fundamentally isn’t the Joker, and the performance is like one tier above Jared Leto’s (this isn’t a compliment to either of them). He’s so Reddit moderator “SOCIETY BAD” I cannot fucking stand it. The performance is certainly not good enough to justify the wave of bullshit method actors who took inspiration from him and this might be incredibly unfair to say, but if the bugger didn’t die then no one would talk about him in this way There’s maybe 5% sauce throughout the entire film but having Gotham just be Chicago is wildly dull - my fiancée and I made the joke that if you could swap out Batman with Optimus Prime and nothing changes in terms of the the city’s aesthetic then you’ve really fucked up. This Batman is far too militaristic and passé about everything that I truly cannot excuse this film’s faults. The copaganda is insane - obviously there’s gonna be cops in a Batman movie but this film makes the point that Batman cannot function without them which is insane. I do not like The Dark Knight and I truly do not understand how people like it as a crime film, as a Batman film, and as one of the supposed best films of all time.

Unpopular opinion: I liked the first movie more, and I couldn’t really get into this one because of the new Rachel. I also think the Joker is a pretty overrated character. I guess I’ve realized that these kinds of movies just aren’t really my thing.
